context: The book revisits an IDC Retail Insights report: the future of marketing will rely heavily on omnichannel strategy, and the ideal shopping experience moves easily across physical and digital platforms. The report predicts that retailers who use cross-channel strategies well can lift customer loyalty by 10%, with profit growth larger still.
q: A retail chain is weighing an investment in cross-channel integration. Based on the report's forecast, what profit growth is most likely?
options: About 3%
About 10%
About 35%
About 150%
explain: The report says retailers that use cross-channel strategies well can grow profits by up to 35%, more than the 10% loyalty gain; the book uses this to argue omnichannel is retail's future.
source: Ch. 1: The Customer Experience Era: The Omnichannel Experience

context: Discussing agile organizations, the book cites Verizon's 2017 Data Breach Investigations Report: more than 80% of breaches trace back to weak or stolen logins and credentials. Today, employees routinely access company cloud services from home or on the go, on all kinds of devices.
q: Your company is rolling out remote and mobile work on a tight security budget. Following the book's advice, what should come first?
options: Enterprise identity management with multi-factor authentication
More firewalls and intrusion detection network equipment
A full ban on using personal devices for any work tasks
Company-wide security awareness talks every quarter
explain: Since most breaches come from credentials, the book recommends enterprise identity policies plus multi-factor authentication via app, SMS, or preset questions to cut identity-verification risk directly.
source: Ch. 1: Becoming an Agile Organization

context: The book cites Google's mobile web research: users are very impatient, and if a page doesn't load within a certain number of seconds, more than half simply leave. The same data shows that across 900K mobile sites worldwide, the average page takes 22 seconds to load.
q: You're setting a mobile load-time ceiling for a brand's campaign page so you don't lose more than half your visitors. Based on this research, what threshold is closest?
options: Ten seconds
Eight seconds
Five seconds
Three seconds
explain: The book states that 53% of users abandon a mobile page that doesn't open within three seconds, and most sites are far slower than that.
source: Ch. 1: Tech as a Catalyst: Change and the Foreseeable Future

context: The book cites a Dentsu Japan study comparing two buys: mobile ads alone versus out-of-home (OOH) plus mobile ads. OOH means ads people encounter outside the home, such as billboards and transit media; the book stresses that OOH can create communication synergy with digital media.
q: You want to convince a client to add OOH on top of mobile ads. Which statement best matches the book's conclusion from this study?
options: OOH mainly adds reach and does little for ad memory
Combined, ad recall rose about 2.2x and clicks rose too
Combined, clicks rose but recall matched mobile alone
OOH distracts people and actually lowers mobile clicks
explain: The study showed that combining OOH with mobile ads raised ad recall 2.2x and click performance 1.6x, helping both memory and action.
source: Ch. 1: A Fresh Start for OOH

context: The book analyzes Taiwan's OOH media: even with population growth stalled, urbanization and the expansion of MRT and high-speed rail nearly doubled total public transit ridership in ten years. Yet transit and outdoor media's share of ad spend fell rather than rose, which the book blames on infrastructure problems such as opaque inventory information.
q: You're explaining to a client the gap between soaring reach and flat ad spend. Per the book's data, how much did total ridership on Taiwan's major public transit systems most plausibly grow in 2017 versus ten years earlier?
options: About 15%
About 40%
About 86%
About 250%
explain: The book says total ridership grew 86% over ten years, yet OOH's share of ad volume actually fell 1%, so the growth in reach never showed up in ad investment.
source: Ch. 1: A Fresh Start for OOH

context: The book explains how machine learning is changing creative: Google's Director Mix can mass-produce and serve video ads whose message matches the video a viewer is watching. During a warm Australian winter in 2016, with soup sales sluggish, Campbell's used it to push “soup suits every occasion.” For example, people watching Beyoncé's “Single Ladies” video saw “Dinner for one?”
q: What change in ad creative does this case best illustrate?
options: One hero ad expanded into thousands of context-tailored versions
Machine learning picks the single best ad to concentrate budget
Demographic targeting with one separate ad for each age group
AI writes the brand proposition and reduces creative headcount
explain: Campbell's used Director Mix to make 1,700 personalized ads served by viewing context, and sales of its Simply Soup line jumped 55.6%.
source: Ch. 2: The Creative Future: Combining Machine Learning

context: Carat proposes “three tracks built as one,” splitting communication into three tracks that work together. The first comes in paid, owned, and earned forms and, like rails and vehicles, carries consumers. The second comes in create, co-create, and curate forms. The third works like a pass that records each consumer's journey.
q: Based on these descriptions, which set most likely names the three tracks, in order?
options: Brand, channel, price
Search, social, e-commerce
Creative, budget, PR
Media, content, data
explain: The book names the three tracks as media, content, and data, which must work together to follow how consumers move and take creativity straight to business.
source: Ch. 2: Media x Content x Data: Three Tracks Built as One Take Creativity Straight to Business

context: On the single-person economy, the book cites 2017 Ministry of the Interior household data: Taiwan's single-person households clearly outnumber two-person households, which make up 19.9%. Among people 15 and older, the share without a spouse is close to 50%. The book sees this wave as a source of new business opportunities.
q: You're sizing the market for single-household products. Based on these clues, what share of all Taiwan households are single-person households most likely to be?
options: About 12%
About 32%
About 19%
About 60%
explain: The book says single-person households number nearly 2.81M, 32.5% of all households in Taiwan, the largest household type.
source: Ch. 3: The Evolution of the Single-Person Economy

context: The book interviews a data scientist at AAA. He says people often picture data scientists as magicians who take the data, apply a model, and get predictions. In reality the work spans data management, cleaning, analysis, and modeling, and actual modeling takes only about 5% of the time, so he jokes he's more of a “data grease monkey.”
q: You're planning hours for a new data project. Based on his account, what share of his time most likely goes to cleaning data?
options: About 80%
About 15%
About 50%
About 95%
explain: He spends about 80% of the time cleaning data, 15% analyzing, and only 5% modeling, so most of the effort goes into getting the data clean.
source: Ch. 6: The Data Scientist

context: The book introduces neuromarketing: data from surveys and interviews often diverges from reality, so Dentsu in Thailand built the “Sappe Happy Meter” to detect happiness, letting women see their own happiness index as they sampled SAPPE BEAUTI DRINK. When they learned the drink had only 50 calories, the index rose even higher.
q: The drink's category is fiercely competitive in Thailand. What result did this campaign, built on the experiment, most likely deliver?
options: Lots of buzz but flat sales, as goodwill didn't convert
Market share doubled from 23% to 47% in three months
Brainwave data contradicted surveys, so it went back to surveys
In a crowded category, share rose from 43% to 47% in one month
explain: The book says the campaign grew SAPPE BEAUTI DRINK's market share from 43% to 47% within one month, a clear gain in a highly competitive market.
source: Ch. 1: Neuromarketing: Do You Really Think Consumers Are Rational?

context: CR-Marketing is the customer-relationship marketing framework the book proposes, grouping members into stages by activity. Once a member's engagement and purchases drop, they slide down a “churn ladder.” The book stresses launching wake-up programs in the sensitive window when members first start loosening their grip, backed by multi-level win-back mechanisms.
q: Following the logic that the lower you go, the harder it is to win members back, what is the churn ladder's most likely order, from mild to severe?
options: Dormant, distant, wavering, churned
Wavering, distant, dormant, churned
Distant, wavering, dormant, churned
Wavering, dormant, distant, churned
explain: The book's chart says to keep members off the churn ladder: wavering > distant > dormant > churned. The earlier you step in, the easier the win-back.
source: Ch. 4: A New Take on CRM in the Big Data Era: CR-Marketing

context: In its 2025 Business Inspiration Forecast, Dentsu Aegis Network says Taiwan becomes a super-aged society after 2025, meaning more than one in five people are 65 or older. The book also notes a widening wealth gap and the lasting appeal of affordable, high-value products, and boldly applies the 80/20 rule to estimate older consumers' spending power.
q: A brand is planning premium products for after 2025. Following the book's reasoning, which judgment is most sound?
options: Older people mostly care about price, so premium goods should go budget
Premium spending stays with the young, so older buyers just need upkeep
Older people, about 20% of the population, may drive 80% of premium spend
Older people spend mainly on health care and add little to other categories
explain: The book says over 20% of people will be 65 or older, and by the 80/20 rule they may account for 80% of high-end spending.
source: Ch. 2: 2025 Business Inspiration Forecast

context: The book cites a 2018 MIT Sloan Management Review survey: an overwhelming majority of CEOs worldwide see digital transformation as the most important and urgent issue, yet those with a clear plan and enough funding to carry it out are fewer than a third of that group. There's a wide gap between “feeling urgent” and “actually doing it.”
q: Based on these clues, which pair of shares (“see it as most urgent” / “have a clear plan”) is most plausible?
options: 50% see it as urgent, 40% have a clear plan
75% see it as urgent, 50% have a clear plan
30% see it as urgent, 10% have a clear plan
90% see it as urgent, 25% have a clear plan
explain: The book says 90% of CEOs worldwide see digital transformation as most important and urgent, but only 25% have a clear plan and enough funding, a reminder that transformation can't stop at slogans.
source: CEO's Talk: Flying Has Never Been a Choice

context: In a full tech audit in 2009, DBS Bank found that heavy tech outsourcing not only weakened its own capabilities in key technologies but also created huge outsourcing costs. The bigger worry: without a solid underlying tech architecture, innovation cycles can't speed up. DBS's vision was to become “a tech company that delivers joyful banking.”
q: If your company faced the same situation, what is the most sensible first step of transformation, following DBS's approach?
options: Spend years investing in infrastructure and tech talent to bring core tech in-house
Hand everything to a bigger systems vendor to get things launched fastest
Launch several innovative apps to grab the market, then fix the foundation later
Restructure the org and KPIs first, keeping the current outsourced tech setup
explain: DBS spent five years, from 2009 to 2014, building its tech foundation, cutting outsourcing's share of tech costs from 85% to 15%, and only then sped up innovation.
source: Keys to Digital Transformation Success: Lessons from DBS Bank

context: The book likens a traditional company to building blocks: each block is an employee, stacked into departments and management layers that grow taller and harder to rearrange. The author observes that companies that transform successfully all manage to turn “blocks” into “LEGO.” LEGO bricks have studs and holes that lock tightly together, and modules can be freely recombined without collapsing.
q: By this metaphor, which kind of employee best fits the book's “LEGO-type employee”?
options: Highly skilled and hits their own KPIs, but cares little about other teams
Knows the company's vision and transformation timeline; helps and works with others
Senior and versed in every approval step, making sure procedures are flawless
Strong executor who completes every order, but never asks about direction or why
explain: The book says LEGO-type employees know the company's vision, goals, and transformation timeline and help one another, so the organization can regroup quickly; block-type employees only look out for themselves.
source: Why Internal Communication Matters in Digital Transformation

context: In the book, an agency leader reads a client's internal handbook that splits client–agency work into four stages: “Transparent” still uses the agency's tools but demands auditability; “Build in-house” builds its own buying ecosystem and no longer needs an agency; “Misty” looks only at results, not process; “Hybrid” has the agency on-site while the client starts copying its expertise.
q: Ordered from least to most client control over media operations, what is the most logical sequence of these four stages?
options: Transparent → Misty → Hybrid → Build in-house
Misty → Hybrid → Transparent → Build in-house
Misty → Transparent → Hybrid → Build in-house
Transparent → Hybrid → Misty → Build in-house
explain: The handbook lays out four steps from agency to build in-house: Misty, Transparent, Hybrid, Build in-house. So the author says bluntly that, to clients, an agency exists to make itself unnecessary.
source: The Last “Have-To” for Agency Leaders

context: German knife brand Zwilling owned several kitchen brands through acquisitions, but they lacked connection, leaving marketing fragmented. Isobar built a creative platform around “endless inspiration for cooking,” using interactive tech and a membership system to unite all its brands. In the same period, the platform gained 50,000+ new users and online transaction value rose 6.9%.
q: The book presents this case as an example of synergy from integration. Based on these clues, how much did total sales most likely rise within three months?
options: About 5%
About 15%
About 200%
About 50%
explain: The book says total sales rose 51% within just three months of launch, far more than the rise in online transactions alone, showing the integration paid off across all channels.
source: Facing Digital Transformation: How Do You Hit the Mark?

context: Dentsu Kuohua wanted media agencies to know Yahoo Oath's digital solutions better. The team observed: agencies sit through dull sales visits all the time; they have many partners to choose from and often decide on price when services look alike; and the best way to build an emotional bond is through the stickiest item in daily life, the cup people hold from morning to night.
q: Based on these insights, which approach best matches the book's solution?
options: Open coffee pop-ups at several big agencies, using custom coffees to promote each content service
Offer better commissions and pricing terms to win deals on price
Hold a large product briefing that covers every digital solution in full
Mail polished product catalogs and case-study booklets to every media planner
explain: The team ran the 9-day “Oath Mobile Coffee Pop-up” at Taiwan's five largest media agencies, reaching nearly 2,000 media planners and buyers and creating 15,000+ business opportunities.
source: Move Human Nature, Transform Business

context: Dentsu Kuohua ran in-depth interviews for PS4 and found price was often just a verbal excuse: young people spend freely on things they believe in. What really blocked purchases was social friction. First, partners felt gaming “wastes the whole day and leaves no time for me,” so gamers wanted to buy but didn't dare. Second, peer pressure: friends chatted about new titles in group chats and they couldn't join in.
q: For gamers with partners, what is the most sensible next communication strategy?
options: Deepen discounts and offer zero-interest installments so gamers have no excuse left
Have gaming KOLs livestream new titles to directly boost gamers' desire to buy
Skip talking to gamers and tell girlfriends a PS4 keeps boyfriends happily at home
Launch a couples' bundle, pitching it as something two people can play at home
explain: The book chose to make a special appeal to girlfriends with “the trick to keeping your boyfriend happily at home,” plus peer pressure, and hit the one-month sales goal in under a week.
source: Move Human Nature, Transform Business

context: The book notes that audiences always want to skip ads, and the wave of ad blocking has left advertisers at a loss. Streaming platforms like Netflix push ad-free viewing, FOX planned to air just 2 minutes of ads per hour of programming by 2020, and Universal Pictures moved to cut prime-time ads by 20%. So the author argues brands should step into the storylines of film and TV content.
q: According to eMarketer, which estimate of the share of US users with ad blockers installed in 2017 is most plausible?
options: About 3%
About 27%
About 55%
About 80%
explain: The book says 27% of US users had installed ad blockers by 2017. Not a majority, but enough to shake up interruptive ads, which is why it argues for weaving brands into content.
source: Unskippable, Unblockable, Unstoppable

context: The book imagines a future where AI home assistants filter information for consumers, and algorithms may flatten brand differences, for example failing to tell a five-century-old single malt whisky from a recently risen newcomer. Rather than letting consumers say “give me a whisky,” brands must build “brand nomination” early so people say the brand's name themselves.
q: Following the book's argument, which approach best keeps a whisky brand from being filtered out by algorithms?
options: Pour money into search and programmatic ads to rank higher in recommendations
Run price promotions to spike short-term sales so algorithms rank it as popular
Optimize keywords for voice assistants so the AI says the brand name first
Hold real-world experiences tied to local culture, and build a member list
explain: The book cites The Balvenie: in 2018 it toured five cities in Taiwan with local craftspeople, drawing 38,000+ participants, and used real-world events to build a member base it can still reach directly.
source: How Can Brands Break Through a World Run by Algorithms?

context: The book says Gen Z prefers visuals. Analysis by Google and Ipsos found Gen Z uses videos to gain knowledge and learn skills they'll need later, and treats watching videos together as a way to bond with family and friends and to de-stress. A Dentsu Taiwan survey shows over 60% of 16- to 21-year-olds keep using a brand once they find one they love.
q: You're building a new brand for Gen Z. What is the most sensible lead platform and approach?
options: Lead with YouTube: authentic videos viewers learn something from
Lead with a Facebook page: brand community posts and giveaways
Lead with a LINE official account: regular coupons and member alerts
Lead with forums like PTT: word-of-mouth posts and discussion threads
explain: Citing several research firms, the book says YouTube is Gen Z's favorite and most-visited platform, so brands should meet their needs with authentic video content.
source: Read Gen Z's Intentions to Win the Future Consumer Market

context: The book introduces the “caveman effect”: prehistoric remains survived mostly in caves, so researchers wrongly assumed early humans mostly lived in caves. In marketing, it means analyzing only the digital data you can collect while ignoring hard-to-capture factors like environment and psychology. Case: consultants used search volume, buzz, and GA to review an OTC nail-fungus drug and found every metric down. Nail fungus is mainly caused by fungal infection.
q: The client is alarmed by the report. From the book's perspective, what is the most sensible next step?
options: Boost the digital ad budget right away to win back search volume and buzz
Switch consultants and rerun the data with more digital analytics tools
Check external factors like local weather first, then run store intercepts and surveys
Rework brand creative and have influencers repackage the product's image
explain: Checking Central Weather Bureau data, the team found rainy days fell nearly 30% from the year before, so fewer people had symptoms; the book also recommends store exit interviews and surveys to find the real barriers to purchase.
source: Data Helps You Understand Consumers, but Do You Really?

context: E.SUN Bank once judged by hand which loan keywords drove conversions. It was slow and laborious, and they often found out six months or a year later that results fell short. The book notes that consumer purchase journeys are no longer a linear funnel. E.SUN then adopted data-driven attribution (DDA), which compares how much each touchpoint in the purchase journey contributes to the final conversion.
q: After adopting DDA, which finding is E.SUN Bank most likely to have made?
options: Nearly all conversions came from users searching E.SUN's brand name directly
Early generic-term searches strongly shaped which brand consumers chose next
Competitor keywords drove the most conversions, so it should bid more on them
Keywords matter little to conversion, so all budget should go to display ads
explain: The book says nearly 60% of conversion credit came from non-brand generic terms; E.SUN promptly adjusted its keyword strategy and its conversion rate rose 42%.
source: Master Data and Use Machine Learning to Mine New Opportunities

context: During the pandemic, Carat positioned brands with its “crisis relevance vs. market demand matrix”: one axis is how relevant a product is to the pandemic, the other is whether demand is rigid (must-buy) or elastic (optional). Products with high relevance and rigid demand fall into the “surge market,” the panic economy/hoarding economy. At that point, consumers care most about whether they can get the product, and watch closely for brands cashing in on the crisis.
q: The disinfecting products you manage sit in the surge market, and demand is exploding in stores and online. Per Carat's advice, what is the most reasonable next step?
options: Keep supply and service steady, and don't raise prices
Raise prices to turn the demand spike into profit
Add discounts to grab share while buying is hot
Switch ads to brand image films and skip the product
explain: Carat's first piece of advice for the surge market is to keep service quality and supply normal and not raise prices, so consumers don't feel the brand is profiteering from disaster.
source: From Black Swans to Gray Rhinos: The Adaptability Quotient Every Brand Needs

context: A.R.I.S.E. is Carat's set of five adaptability quotients: agility (sensing market shifts fast), association (linking the brand to hot topics), innovation (breaking the existing business model), share of heart (managing the brand's place in consumers' minds), and experience (getting every point where consumers touch the brand right). During the pandemic, several night markets launched dedicated delivery riders: customers could combine orders from different stalls and order by phone or LINE for home delivery, solving two pain points, “going out” and “queuing to pick up food.”
q: Within the book's framework, which adaptability quotient does the night markets' move mainly strengthen?
options: Agility
Association
Share of heart
Experience
explain: The book files night-market delivery under experience: brand experience is an overall feeling, not a single touchpoint, and the night markets redesigned the flow from ordering to pickup so people could enjoy their food safely at home.
source: From Black Swans to Gray Rhinos: The Adaptability Quotient Every Brand Needs

context: Drawing on “Car Psychology,” the book groups Taiwan car buyers' psychological decision-making into seven factors: status symbol, passenger comfort, safety, speed, space, parking, and fuel efficiency. Comparing the Mercedes-Benz GLC factor by factor with the models it is most often compared to, the GLC shows a strong edge in space and fuel efficiency, but has lots of room to improve on safety and speed.
q: If you were a Mercedes-Benz marketer, what is the most reasonable next step based on this analysis?
options: Push space and fuel efficiency harder to widen the lead
Plan ads, KOLs, or events to talk up safety and speed
Cut prices to make up for lagging psychological factors
Boost digital buzz first, then adjust the message later
explain: The book suggests marketers analyze how to improve the lagging factors, thinking through safety and speed and whether ads, KOLs, or events are the best way to strengthen communication with consumers.
source: The Super Salesperson's Secret Weapon

context: The book treats “comparisons ÷ digital mentions” as a brand's conversion rate: being talked about online is only a start, being put on a shopper's comparison list is closer to a sale, and a higher ratio means better performance. In the period analyzed, BMW had the most digital mentions but a ratio of just 0.66; Audi was 1.43; Lexus had the fewest mentions but a ratio of 3.91; Mercedes-Benz itself was 1.34.
q: If you were a Mercedes-Benz marketer, which approach is most worth studying first?
options: Study how BMW creates the most digital buzz
Study how Audi balances buzz and comparisons
Study how Lexus turns little buzz into many comparisons
Boost digital buzz first to out-mention BMW
explain: The book notes that BMW had the most digital mentions but ranked last in comparisons, and urges Mercedes-Benz marketers to quickly analyze what Lexus does to convert so well.
source: The Super Salesperson's Secret Weapon

context: Isobar cites Salesforce's customer research: customers don't want to deal separately with a brand's marketing, sales, and service teams; they want a brand that understands their needs, and they're willing to be loyal to it. Another study in the same chapter says nearly 80% of customers expect the brand to know who they are right away in every interaction.
q: Based on these clues, what is the most plausible estimate for the share of customers who say a brand's content, interactions, and service at every touchpoint matter as much as the product itself?
options: About 20%
About 40%
About 60%
Over 80%
explain: The book states that 84% of customers feel this way, which is Isobar's starting point for recommending that brands adopt marketing technology and unify customer data to improve the experience.
source: Using Salesforce to Unify Brand Data, Improve Customer Experience, and Drive Growth

context: After Isobar helps a brand unify its real-name customer data in Salesforce, marketers can first “define the audience,” then “define the task,” and set rules so the system sends messages automatically when conditions are met. The book's example audience: prospects who picked up a free sample and also joined the brand's LINE account. They're interested in the product but haven't actually ordered.
q: For this group, which automated message best fits the book's approach?
options: Send a 3-day coupon that leads them to order online
Send a monthly brand newsletter to build goodwill
Text the same discount to every member for reach
Wait for a store visit and have staff recommend it
explain: The book's example sends exactly these prospects a coupon valid for three days that leads them to the e-commerce site. After Isobar launched 10/10's new membership program, it hit 8,880 LINE friends in week one, and Q1 2020 sales rose 30% over the same period in 2019.
source: Using Salesforce to Unify Brand Data, Improve Customer Experience, and Drive Growth

context: iProspect proposes the “Search 4V”: voice search, visual search, vertical search (in-site search on e-commerce and social platforms), and various (blended) search. The book observes that older people type slowly and younger people want to ask the moment a need pops up, both driving voice search; and when people search by voice, they talk as if to a person, phrasing their need as a “question.”
q: Your health supplement brand wants to show up in voice search results. How should you adjust your site content?
options: Pack pages with more short keywords to raise density
Buy more SEM keywords to cover it with paid slots
Use an FAQ structure that answers common questions
Add alt tags to product images so they're easier to find
explain: The book recommends finding people's voice search phrases through search intent research, then using an FAQ content structure so crawlers can index brand content more easily and the brand can own the voice search results page. Alt tags belong to visual search optimization.
source: Outpacing Rivals in Digital: The New Era of the “Search 4V” Is Here

context: Vizeum breaks media communication into Channel, Content, Context, and Connection, where Context means finding the moment consumers are most receptive. Take the cat parasite drop “All-in-One Cat”: client research says mosquito-borne heartworm is 99% fatal in cats, and mosquitoes get indoors too. But YouTube viewers see hundreds of ads a day and may skip at any moment.
q: Planning YouTube video ads for All-in-One Cat, which approach best fits the book's thinking?
options: One 30-second brand film, same version for all owners
Swap intros by humidity or location, naming the product first
Fully explain heartworm risk first, reveal the product at the end
Lead with a limited-time discount to get owners to click
explain: The book first used data to define potential owners' viewing contexts, prepared multiple custom intros, served them automatically on signals such as rising humidity or being near a vet clinic, and named the product right in the intro, so even viewers who didn't finish still built awareness.
source: How Media Performance Connects to Sales Targets

context: In the ACM automated ad-creation platform that Dentsu Kuohua brought in, the AI creative ADAM picks layouts, visuals, and copy to assemble banners based on preset conditions, predicts click-through rates to rank them, and hands them to creatives for final polish. The traditional process from internal brief to finished banner takes at least several days; the book says that with ADAM, an agency can take on “hundreds of banners within 30 minutes.”
q: Based on this clue, what is the most plausible estimate of how long ADAM takes to produce one banner?
options: About five seconds
About five minutes
About thirty minutes
About half a day
explain: Hundreds in 30 minutes means just a few seconds each. The book says ADAM produces one banner every five seconds, and creatives then pick the better-performing ones to refine.
source: AI X Creativity

context: In early 2020, Google announced Chrome would phase out third-party cookies, so brands could no longer track individuals across sites with cookies that other sites drop in the browser. The direction of Google's Privacy Sandbox: data in principle stays on the user's device, the browser decides how much to reveal, and identification is by “groups” rather than “individuals.”
q: Facing this shift, which way of reaching audiences is least affected?
options: Switch to fingerprinting to keep identifying people across sites
Keep buying third-party audience lists from ad networks
Spend more on cross-site personalized retargeting
Use contextual targeting plus first-party data from your own site
explain: The book says contextual targeting and first-party data targeting are unaffected, because they only use your own users' interactions on your site. New techniques like fingerprinting may not follow privacy protection rules.
source: The Death of Third-Party Cookie Marketing

context: Taiwan officially became an aged society in 2018, and three major chronic diseases alone take about 15% of national health insurance spending. After interviewing consumers, the book found self-managed health is “easy to know, hard to do”: habits take a long time to form and results are hard to see, and with long working hours and stress, many people give up halfway. Only 34% of people meet the standard for regular exercise.
q: A sports brand wants to help consumers keep up healthy behavior. Which approach best fits the opportunity the book sees?
options: Launch high-intensity training so results show faster
Build a community where users support and join each other
Run lots of ads stressing why regular exercise matters
Offer a one-time health check discount to draw people in
explain: The book lists “start from community and create change with users” as one of the opportunities, noting that communities are key to sustaining behavior change and building emotional ties, such as Giant's Ride Life platform and Space Cycle, which moved spin classes into nightclubs.
source: Tech-Empowered: The Big Health Wave Arrives

context: The book notes that understanding consumers used to rely mostly on surveys or interviews, which only show what people “say”; now digital footprints from the web and e-commerce show what they “do.” Dentsu Japan once worked with an e-commerce partner to track which foods a group of self-described health-conscious people actually bought online.
q: Which set is most likely the top three foods this group bought online?
options: Salad, yogurt, coffee
Rice, veggie juice, milk
Instant noodles, energy drinks, beer
Bread, tea drinks, chocolate
explain: The book says the top three were instant noodles, energy drinks, and beer, all high-calorie, showing that behavioral data fills in the gap between self-image and behavior that surveys miss.
source: Marketing Measurement Decoded

context: The book uses Google's consumer mobility data to track Taiwan during the pandemic. After the nationwide Level 3 alert on May 19, 2021, foot traffic vanished from shopping districts and department stores as people went into a self-imposed “quasi-lockdown.” The book reads the drop in public transit as “more than half of users” switching to other transport or no longer riding because their companies moved to working from home, though many essential commuters remained.
q: Based on these clues, how far had public transit use fallen one week after the Level 3 alert (5/26)?
options: About 16%
About 36%
About 56%
About 76%
explain: The book says public transit use fell 56% on 5/26, and infers that working from home sharply lengthened the time consumers spent at home.
source: Consumer Resources and Opportunities Hidden in the Pandemic

context: Dentsu's Consumer Communication Survey (CCS) tracks agreement with “I'm willing to save up to buy what I want”: 67.2% in 2018, 66.1% in 2019, and an even sharper drop in 2020. The book also notes that the pandemic made people feel how unpredictable life is and rethink what life means.
q: Given this trend, which reading and response makes the most sense for a brand?
options: Consumers are less patient for what they want; seize the moment to convert
Consumers are more cautious and frugal; push long-term saving and installments
Consumer spending power has shrunk; cut prices across the board to win budgets
It's only a few points; normal fluctuation, so no change in strategy is needed
explain: The book says the share fell to 64.2% in 2020, meaning consumers want to buy now and own it, so brands should seize the golden moment of “instant gratification.”
source: Consumer Resources and Opportunities Hidden in the Pandemic (Instant Gratification)

context: Consumer Vision 2030 predicts “zero emissions from companies, zero tolerance from consumers.” Citing a global survey, the book says 66% of consumers believe that by 2030, corporate reputations will rest on efforts against climate change. As consumers cut waste in their own lives, they will hold brands to the same strict standards.
q: A beverage brand wants to protect its reputation through 2030. Per the book, which approach best answers these consumers?
options: Hold a big beach cleanup each year to boost green exposure
Switch to eco packaging and promote the change heavily in ads
Buy carbon credits to offset emissions, keep production as is
Audit impact from materials to production to use, and improve it
explain: The book says consumers will make sure products cause no harm to the environment from production through use, so one-off image events or offsets won't pass this “zero tolerance” test.
source: Crossing 2030: Climate Change, Brand Upgrade

context: The book's “New Paradigm for Data Governance” notes that pandemic-era health and movement tracking, plus iOS 14 asking users whether apps may track them, sharply raised awareness of personal data. Dentsu's Digital Society Index Survey 2020 found that worrying about having less control over personal data in 2030 than now is a majority concern, though not a universal one.
q: Based on these clues, what share of consumers most likely agree they'll have less control over their personal data in 2030 than now?
options: About 19%
About 69%
About 39%
About 96%
explain: The book says nearly seven in ten (69%) consumers agree they'll have less control over their data in the future, which is why it predicts the rise of personal data assistants and digital ethics rules.
source: Crossing 2030: A New Paradigm for Data Governance

context: The book argues that a company's social impact is a mid- to long-term commitment, not a short-term tactic. In 2018 Dentsu chose Laomei in Shimen District, New Taipei: its economy had declined and many children were raised by grandparents, but it had tourism potential such as the green algae reef. Aiming to revive the local economy, Dentsu worked through the teachers and students of Laomei Elementary and, starting from stories the children created together, launched the four-year “Take Off, Xiaomei!” project.
q: Given these conditions, what outcome did the project most likely end with?
options: A digital learning center at the school with online courses
A tourism mascot for Laomei with co-branded local souvenirs
Kids' stories painted on town walls: a multimedia storybook town
A rural livestream e-commerce base to help sell local produce
explain: The book says the project began with the children's co-created picture books and used town murals combined with local culture, AR experiences, and tourist routes to build Taiwan's first multimedia storybook town.
source: Building Social Impact

context: According to Hootsuite and We Are Social's “Digital 2020” report, the global average time online is 6 hr 43 min a day. The book notes that Taiwan ranks near the top among many countries, with people spending about one-third of their day online, half of it on mobile.
q: Based on these clues, which is closest to the average daily time people in Taiwan spend online?
options: About 8 hours
About 6.5 hours
About 5 hours
About 10 hours
explain: The book says people in Taiwan average 7 hr 57 min online a day, 1 hr 14 min more than the global average, so being online is now a “baseline” of daily life.
source: The Last Mile into the New Normal

context: Set in a household registration office, Sinyi Realty's “Trust and Happiness” ad tells a love story that moves from doubt to trust amid pandemic anxiety, without directly selling the company's services. It went on to win Taiwan's first Cannes Entertainment Lions Grand Prix. Sinyi always post-tests its ads; the past KPI was for 20–30% of viewers to have a better view of the brand afterward. The chief strategy officer said this ad's result was “beyond expectations.”
q: Based on these clues, what share of viewers most likely had a better view of the brand in the post-test?
options: About 25%
About 35%
About 50%
About 70%
explain: Sinyi's chief strategy officer Chou Chuang-yun said this ad reached 70%, far above the past 20–30% KPI, making it “the most successful ad in our history.”
source: Crossing Hearts: How a Story About “Trust” Won the Cannes Grand Prix

context: The book breaks the consumer journey down with ISRPE: I is learning something new (Interest), S is seeking a solution (Search), R is comparing options (Research), P is buying (Purchase), and E is sharing the experience (Experience). It warns that a common brand mistake is not building strategy around the search intent at each stage, and simply pouring budget into traffic and conversions.
q: A consumer searches “robot vacuum brand A vs brand B, which is better.” Under ISRPE, what stage are they in, and what should the brand offer most?
options: Interest stage: raise awareness with brand image ads
Research stage: offer spec comparisons and honest reviews
Purchase stage: push a limited-time discount to close
Experience stage: invite them to leave a usage review
explain: Comparing two brands is the Research (comparing options) stage; the book argues for setting content direction by each stage's search intent rather than always pushing promotions.
source: Deconstructing the Consumer Journey with Search Data

context: Consumer Vision 2030's “Star-Rating System” predicts that the reputation economy will fully mature: companies will rate customers by their behavior and offer differentiated service. For example, Airbnb hosts ignore guests with many bad reviews, and Uber in Australia has begun refusing riders rated below four stars. The book also notes that Taiwan consumers already support loyalty programs and expect their spending to be rewarded in kind.
q: A coffee chain wants to respond to this trend. Per the book, which approach makes the most sense?
options: Cut prices across the board so every customer gets the same deal
Spend big on a celebrity endorser to boost brand awareness first
Build member tiers based on behavior and give tiered rewards
Drop the membership program to avoid controversy over customer data
explain: Dentsu CCS shows 72.9% of Taiwan consumers like buying from or using brands that reward loyal customers, so the book predicts brand-led rating and reward systems will become mainstream.
source: Crossing 2030: The Star-Rating System

context: The book says Red Bull understands that every consumer has a shifting, “kaleidoscope” identity: caring about different topics at different times and curious about different people and things. So it turned itself into a kaleidoscope too, owning its own TV channel, magazines, film production company, and music studios. Staff joke that it feels less like a drinks company and more like a studio in the culture industry.
q: Given this positioning, what visual order is Red Bull's website homepage most likely to use?
options: New flavors first, then events, and video content last
Limited-time promos first, then athletes, and products last
Classic can design first, then brand history and retail info
Red Bull TV first, then events and athletes, and products last
explain: The book says the site leads with Red Bull TV, then events and athletes, and only then products, echoing the idea that “Red Bull is a culture company that just happens to sell drinks.”
source: Deconstructing the Kaleidoscope of Motives to Give Brand Value Concrete Form

context: The book sees media as ultimately just a tool: an amplifier that starts from “trust.” Its example: when Tesla interviewed salespeople, it told candidates “Sell me a Tesla.” Everyone talked specs and design, but the interviewer asked back, “Why didn't anyone ask who I am?” Mercedes-Benz, by contrast, excels at traditional big-media marketing, and the gap in the two brands' average ad spend per car is so large the book asks outright, “Why is there such a gap?”
q: Mercedes-Benz spends about US$926 on ads per car. Based on these clues, what is Tesla's figure most likely to be?
options: About US$6
About US$300
About US$900
About US$2,000
explain: Data cited in the book puts Tesla's average ad spend at just US$6 per car, showing that digital transformation starts from the consumer's point of view and trust, not from buying big media.
source: Media Tech Always Comes from Human Nature

context: Consumer Vision 2030's “Super Humans” trend means new technology will enhance people's physical and mental abilities and extend lifespans, changing even how we define a “person,” so brands must adjust their channels, content, and communication strategies. The book specifically warns that marketing language and labels need careful thought, because labels can have positive or negative effects.
q: A health brand is launching a new product for people 65 and over. Per the book, which communication approach should it avoid most?
options: Center it on hobbies and life goals, showing an active daily life
Print “for the elderly only” in large type, stressing it's for seniors
Stress real benefits for physical strength and mental health
Offer online customer service and digital buying to simplify purchase
explain: The book says seniors don't like being called “elders” or “old people,” and products labeled “for the elderly only” put them off even more.
source: Crossing 2030: Super Humans

context: The book notes that from iOS 14.5, Apple rolled out ATT (apps must get user consent before tracking them), making it ever harder for brands to reach consumers precisely. Per the WSJ, half a year after the policy took effect, advertisers shifted budgets heavily to Android: Android mobile ads grew over 10% in the same period, and CPM rose too.
q: Based on these clues, how did advertisers' iOS mobile ad spend most likely change half a year after ATT took effect?
options: Roughly flat, down about 3%
A modest drop of about 10%
A sharp drop of about 33%
Near zero, down about 90%
explain: Citing the WSJ, the book says iOS mobile ad spend fell about 33% as budgets moved heavily to Android, without abandoning iOS entirely.
source: New Assets, New Skills, New Traits: Mastering a Fragmented New World

context: U.S. organic rules require farmland to stop using all chemical fertilizers and pesticides for three straight years before it can be certified organic, and yields drop sharply during that time, so organic farming covers only about 1% of farmland. AB InBev's Michelob Ultra launched the “Pure Gold Contract” to help farmers willing to convert get through that painful period.
q: To get farmers to accept three years of lower yields, which contract design best matches what the book describes?
options: Buy at 25% above the original price for three straight years
Pay a one-time 25% bonus after organic certification
Buy all output at the original price in year one, then at market
Subsidize organic fertilizer while keeping the original price
explain: The contract guaranteed buying at 25% above the original price for three years, covering the whole transition so farmers' livelihoods stayed secure despite lower yields.
source: Modern Creativity: Creating a Business Multiplier Effect for Brands

context: KFC has 5,800 stores in China, about one per 240,000 people, and soaring rents in tier-1 and tier-2 cities make expansion a dilemma. KFC launched the “Pocket Store” on a social platform, letting every user open their own store on their phone, invite friends to order, and pick up at a nearby store.
q: The book calls the result of this no-new-store approach “unprecedented” and notes it eased ordering load at stores. Which outcome is most likely what happened?
options: Lots of buzz; revenue hit about 120% of the annual target
More visits; revenue hit about 300% of the annual target
Orders overloaded stores and the campaign ended early
Visits and revenue surged to 900% of the annual target
explain: The book says the Pocket Store drove visits, eased ordering load at physical stores, and hit an unprecedented 900% of that year's revenue target.
source: Modern Creativity: Creating a Business Multiplier Effect for Brands

context: With third-party cookies about to disappear, brands find it ever harder to reach consumers precisely. Dentsu Taiwan staged an online “exorcism” launch event for Yahoo, portraying a cookieless world as an age overrun by demons. Four demons stood for four problems tied to data, tracking, and media, which Yahoo's four “Truly Connect” solutions then subdued.
q: Thinking about the problems of a cookieless world, which “demon” is least likely to have appeared at this event?
options: Hidden Princess: makes consumers vanish
Amnesia Ghost: makes consumers forget brands
Face-Blind Fiend: blurs consumer profiles
Layout-Lock Demon: restricts online and offline media
explain: The book's four demons are the Hidden Princess, the Mad Hacker, the Face-Blind Fiend, and the Layout-Lock Demon, covering tracking, personal data, profiles, and media. Brands being forgotten isn't a problem caused directly by losing cookies.
source: Modern Creativity: The Multiplier Power of the Unimagined

context: Dentsu's CCS (Consumer Connection System, a long-running study of Taiwanese consumers' life values) found that after the pandemic, age 40 became a dividing line in how people see the present and future. Workers 40+ are often managers and family breadwinners, carrying pressure for results and organizational change; those 39 and under are at home with digital tech and pursue self-fulfillment.
q: Given this, what trend did the share of each age group “satisfied with their quality of life” most likely show from 2018 to 2021?
options: Both rose, with a smaller rise for 40+
Both fell, with a bigger drop for 39 and under
40+ fell while 39 and under rose
40+ rose while 39 and under fell
explain: CCS data show workers 40+ fell from 47% to 43%, while those 39 and under rose from 43% to 47%, so the two lines crossed.
source: New Markets Driving New Future Value for Brands

context: Kantar surveyed 500 people in Taiwan in Q1 2022: nearly 70% believe their small choices can change the world, yet 76% say everyday convenience and cost keep them from acting more sustainably. The book sorts this attitude-action gap into six barriers: price, information, convenience, sense of responsibility, impact, and availability.
q: You're launching an eco-friendly product and want to tackle the barrier the most respondents share first. Based on the survey, which should come first?
options: Thinking eco-friendly products cost more
Companies not giving enough information
Most stores not carrying eco-friendly products
Seeing it as companies' job, not consumers'
explain: 85% think eco-friendly products cost more, the most common barrier; 71% cite a lack of information, and fewer point to corporate responsibility or availability.
source: Sustainable Transformation: Seize the Trends, Break New Ground

context: The book's “creative scale” sorts creativity into six types: harmful, ignored, good work, creates culture, changes society, and defines the future. Modern Creativity values disruptive innovation: whether an idea spreads as culture, drives positive social change, or leads people to explore the future together, not just whether the work itself is well made.
q: An ad is beautifully produced and wins awards, but sparks no conversation or behavior change. Where does it most likely fall on the creative scale?
options: Creates culture; counts as Modern Creativity
Changes society; counts as Modern Creativity
Ignored; doesn't count as Modern Creativity
Good work; doesn't count as Modern Creativity
explain: The book says only creating culture, changing society, and defining the future count as Modern Creativity; well-made work that changes nothing stays at good work.
source: Modern Creativity: Differentiating Through Disruptive Innovation in Chaotic Times

context: dentsu good says most companies go through three stages of sustainability transformation: an intro stage that launches sustainability projects to comply with laws and policies; a growth stage that builds it into everyday capabilities and culture; and a mature stage that builds differentiation and drives sustainable innovation. Each stage centers on an English word starting with C.
q: A company has already made sustainability part of its culture and next wants it to become an edge rivals can't copy. Which word anchors the stage it's moving into?
options: Compliance
Competitiveness
Competency
Commitment
explain: The book says the intro stage centers on Compliance, the growth stage on Competency, and the mature stage on Competitiveness, which is about building a differentiated competitive edge.
source: Growth through Good: Start with Good, Grow Sustainably

context: Dentsu Japan noticed uneven tuna quality in supermarkets and found that Japan's rapid aging had caused a severe shortage of tuna inspectors, putting its proud grading know-how at risk of dying out. Veteran inspectors judge tuna by the pattern of the tail's cross-section, so the team worked with Toyosu Market to build the world's first tuna inspection database with AI: TUNA SCOPE.
q: The book uses how long it takes to train a professional inspector to show why training alone can't close the gap. Based on these clues, which estimate is most reasonable?
options: About 1 year
About 3 years
At least 10 years
About 5 years
explain: The book says training a professional tuna inspector takes at least 10 years, too slow to keep pace with aging, which is why AI was used to standardize grading and fill the gap.
source: Growth through Good: Start with Good, Grow Sustainably

context: In March 2021, Beeple's NFT artwork “Everydays: The First 5000 Days” sold at Christie's for US$69 million. The book uses it to show how NFTs brought in new buyers who had rarely taken part in the art market; bidding at this level takes both fluency in crypto and digital culture and substantial wealth.
q: Per Christie's breakdown of bidders by age, which generation most likely made up the largest share?
options: Gen Z
Gen X
Baby Boomers
Millennials
explain: Citing Christie's, the book says Millennials made up 58%, followed by Gen X at 33%, Gen Z at 6%, and Baby Boomers at 3%, which is why it says NFTs brought Millennials into the art market.
source: The Power of Web 3.0: Expanding How We Imagine the World

context: Pizza Hut Taiwan built a Taiwanese-flavor brand through “Connected Creative Experiences,” such as a “Pizza Comeback Vote” during election season, and hit its best annual sales in 35 years in 2021. In 2022 it tapped the metaverse buzz, becoming the first Pizza Hut worldwide to release Taiwanese-flavor NFT blind boxes for unreleased flavors. Before the boxes were even opened, resale prices had climbed to dozens of times the original price.
q: Using the “dozens of times” clue, which premium is closest to what these pre-opening trades reached?
options: About 3,900%
About 390%
About 39,000%
About 90%
explain: The book says the blind boxes traded briskly before opening at premiums as high as 3,900%, about 40 times the original price, as an example of the brand continually trying new tech channels.
source: “Connected Creative Experiences” Accelerate Modern Creativity

context: “Five Dilemmas for the CMO” says brands' future battle in media is a visibility war: be found when people search with a purpose (search visibility) and be seen when they scroll without one (social visibility). Algorithms favor content people need, and if an ad is judged unneeded, it can cost several times what rivals pay.
q: Given this, what kind of talent should a marketing team most build up? The book sees it as one of the scarcest new roles ahead.
options: Negotiators who buy media in bulk to push down CPM
People who create content audiences need and want to mention
Ad operators who sharpen targeting and raise frequency
Data engineers who connect first-party data to CRM
explain: The book says the only way to win visibility is to create the content audiences need, and calls people who can do it “Visibility Managers.”
source: Five Dilemmas for the CMO

context: The book cites web analytics firm Similarweb: Microsoft's Bing, with only a 3% share, saw its visits briefly jump after teaming up with ChatGPT and becoming a generative AI search bot. The book calls this merely “gently tapping the legs of Google's throne”: noticeable, but not enough to shake the leader.
q: Based on these clues, which estimate of how much Bing's visits “briefly rose” is most reasonable?
options: About 1.5%
About 15%
About 150%
About 15x
explain: The book says Bing's visits briefly rose 15% after adding ChatGPT: enough to draw attention, but far from doubling, so it only “gently” tapped Google's position.
source: The AI Shift from Content to Communication

context: Coca-Cola's “Masterpiece” ad includes an extremely complex animated sequence handled by Electric Theatre Collective. AI tools sharply cut their timeline, and they said that without AI it might have taken five times as long. That works out to well over half a year for a no-AI version.
q: You are estimating the timeline for an AI-assisted animation project of similar scale. Based on these clues, how long did they actually take?
options: Eight days
Eight months
Eight weeks
Two years
explain: The book says it took just eight weeks; five times that is about 40 weeks. Eight days is too short, and eight months or more would stretch the no-AI version to several years, which doesn't fit the clues.
source: Only People Strive for Excellence

context: Using the 18th-century steam engine, the book explains that a “phenomenal” technology took about 100 years to go from invention to widespread use. It stresses that what decides winners is often not the tech itself but outside conditions: whether capital truly flows in, and whether supports like railways and coal are in place to make the tech the core of the whole production system.
q: Under this framework, which period in the roughly 100 years of steam engine evolution mattered most for whether organizations survived?
options: The first few years of breakthroughs after its invention
The year the first steam-powered factory was built
The transition after it was replaced by newer tech
The last 50 years, after capital flowed in and it became core
explain: The book says the decisive period was the last 50 years: only after interest turned into real capital and steam became the core of production did strategic positioning pay off.
source: Phenomenal Trends Reshaping Future Supply and Demand

context: The book argues that on the consumer side, tech works by removing friction costs in the buying process. Higher productivity makes goods cheaper, longer opening hours and steady supply cut waiting, not having to go out saves effort, and personalized recommendations ease the burden of deciding what to buy.
q: Based on these examples, which set best matches the “four main resources” the book says tech saves consumers?
options: Money, time, physical energy, mental energy
Time, physical energy, skills, emotion
Money, time, connections, taste
Money, physical energy, knowledge, trust
explain: The book's table maps them one by one: lower spending is money, less waiting or fewer stockouts is time, less effort going out to shop is physical energy, and less thinking about what to buy is mental energy.
source: Phenomenal Trends Reshaping Future Supply and Demand

context: The book says AI output is only as good as the data it is fed, and a company's own, continually updated member and transaction data matters most. Companies also need to pick the areas where AI creates value, such as product information, inventory, and customer management, and weigh how much to invest and how fast.
q: A retail brand's boss wants to profit from AI, and the team proposes four directions. Which one is least part of the book's three factors for profiting from AI?
options: Build a first-party database that keeps updating
Map out where AI can create value
Expand influencer partnerships and budgets
Decide how much and how fast to invest in the tech
explain: The book's three factors are a first-party database, where AI is applied to create value, and investment strength; expanding influencer partnerships is a marketing tactic, not one of them.
source: Phenomenal Trends Reshaping Future Supply and Demand

context: Gucci's Chengdu flagship has a three-meter-tall digital mural blending the culture and nature of Florence and Chengdu, with scenes that shift from morning to night. The team, Random Studio, used Midjourney, Stable Diffusion, and DALL-E to generate huge numbers of layers, but blending so many elements into one whole was still a major challenge.
q: From the book's view of human-machine collaboration, what was the key success factor in this case?
options: Letting AI finish the design on its own, with no creative team
Picking the newest, most powerful single AI image tool
Adding more screens in store for more immersion
Human art direction and storytelling tying AI output together
explain: The book says human art direction and storytelling were needed to handle the blending from different angles. The mural, made of 33 large LED screens, shows AI assisting rather than replacing human creativity.
source: Human-Machine Collaboration Defines New Value

context: People on the autism spectrum often struggle to express basic needs such as wanting water or feeling pain, and picture cards have long been used to help. Experts recently found they often have strong interests in specific topics. Brazilian telecom VIVO and DDB launched the “Autism Journey” site: users enter a card name, a character, and what the character is doing, and AI generates cards to choose from.
q: According to the book, why is this site most likely to improve communication?
options: Cards are tailored to the child's interests, so they engage more
AI decides for parents what the child needs
It switches fully to standardized cards to avoid confusion
It has children type instead, gradually replacing cards
explain: The book says turning “a child eating pizza” into personalized cards like “a puppy eating pizza” makes them more appealing, so children engage more and are more motivated to learn. The site shows three cards to choose from each time.
source: Human-Machine Collaboration Defines New Value

context: The book warns that generative AI may produce false content about a brand, and that quality content is the most basic line of defense, so brands should keep providing content that meets Google's E-E-A-T guidelines. E-E-A-T is four measures of content quality: the two Es are first-hand experience and expertise, and the T is trust. The book also notes users will care more and more about who is saying something.
q: A brand wants to strengthen the “A” in E-E-A-T. Which move fits best?
options: Add precise data and a proofreading process to every article
Get respected authors or sites in the field to write or cite it
Mass-produce articles with AI to raise brand exposure
Write catchy headlines to boost clicks and attention
explain: The A is Authority: whether the author or site is an authority in the field. The other options are closer to accuracy, automation, and attention, none of which is an E-E-A-T measure.
source: The AI Shift from Content to Communication

context: Countries are moving at different speeds on generative AI laws, and Europe puts special weight on personal data protection. On March 31, 2023, Italy's data protection authority (Garante) suspended ChatGPT; OpenAI then introduced new rules, and ChatGPT became available in Italy again from April 28.
q: Based on these clues, what kind of rules did OpenAI most likely add so ChatGPT could return?
options: Lower subscription prices to answer complaints of unfair fees
Launch a full Italian interface and customer support
Watermark images generated by AI
Explain how user data is collected and used, and add age checks
explain: The book says the authority cited privacy concerns, especially unclear age controls; access resumed only after OpenAI introduced new rules on collecting and using user data and on age verification.
source: Letting Ideas Soar Within the Rules

context: Countries differ on copyright for AI-generated works. Japan does not protect works generated by AI on its own, and in the US the key is how much a human was involved. Unlike the EU and US, the UK clearly grants copyright, but with conditions, and the protection period counts from the day the work is completed.
q: Your team in the UK uses AI as a tool to create music for an ad and wants to claim copyright. Per the book's summary, which judgment is most reasonable?
options: Anything AI-generated automatically gets copyright
AI-generated works get no protection in the UK
Show human involvement; 50 years of protection from completion
Show human involvement; protection for the author's life plus 70 years
explain: The book says the UK requires showing human involvement, with a human still the author and AI used as a tool; such works get 50 years of copyright protection from completion.
source: Letting Ideas Soar Within the Rules

context: According to Bloomberg Law, copyright infringement is the most common type of generative AI lawsuit. For example, stock photo company Getty Images sued Stability AI, maker of Stable Diffusion, claiming it copied large numbers of images without permission or compensation. Using ChatGPT as an example, the book also notes that model training may use copyrighted text.
q: Your company wants to mass-produce marketing copy with generative AI. Per the book, which move best reduces infringement risk?
options: Prefer models trained on content without copyright
Output is not infringing once a human edits it
Use a big vendor's tool so the vendor bears liability
Label the copy “AI-generated” to avoid liability
explain: The book says using ChatGPT directly may well infringe, but setting up a model trained only on content without copyright is an option worth considering. The Getty suit alleges 12M images were copied without permission.
source: Letting Ideas Soar Within the Rules

context: The book notes that companies first asked employees for intelligence (IQ), then for emotional intelligence (EQ) to keep the workplace stable and communication smooth; in the generative AI era, they must also build “AIQ,” or Dentsu Intelligence. The author also cautions that chasing new tools or building your own should not be the goal, and that consumers will increasingly get information through conversation after conversation with AI.
q: A manager wants to raise the team's AIQ. Based on how the book defines AIQ, which move fits best?
options: Buy top-spec AI computing hardware
Have staff work with AI through daily, repeated dialogue
Require every employee to learn coding and build tools
Rank departments by AI standardized test scores
explain: The book defines AIQ as our ability to get along with AI, and as building a new kind of communication skill. Following on from IQ and EQ, it is about how people interact with AI, not hardware or coding.
source: The Metamorphosis of Dentsu Intelligence: AIQ

context: The book cites Walmart's CEO at the August 2024 earnings call: generative AI is now built into the whole shopping experience, from personalized search and virtual assistants to marketing content. The three "100x" gains he announced all fall in one kind of work: high-volume, repetitive content handling built on text and product data.
q: Based on this clue, which of these is most likely one of the things Walmart said improved 100x?
options: Self-checkout speed in stores
Customer service call pickup speed
Efficiency of updating product info online
Staff scheduling efficiency in stores
explain: The book lists three 100x gains: product info updates online, attribute expansion speed, and less staffing needed for catalog work, all product-content tasks where generative AI shines.
source: Seeing 100 Times the Hope

context: The book argues that the more fragmented marketing gets, the more the brand should sit at the center of all marketing investment. It cites 18 years of Kantar BrandZ tracking: measured from 2006, strong brands' stock prices beat the S&P 500 by 88%, and the stronger the brand, the wider the lead.
q: Looking only at the top 10 strongest brands, what's the most reasonable estimate for the same figure?
options: About 60%
About 130%
About 1,300%
About 88%
explain: The book says the top 10 strongest brands reached as much as 129%, pulling further ahead of the 88% for strong brands overall, which shows that investing in brand value drives lasting growth.
source: Bringing Brand Marketing Up to Date

context: The UNIQLO East District flagship started as a simple store-opening job, but Dentsu mb scaled the frame from one store to the whole district: walking maps, stamp collecting, and co-branded T-shirts with local shops brought young people back to the East District. After opening, the store hit 105% of its sales target, sales grew 166% year over year, and 91% said the store would make them visit the area more often.
q: Based on these results, what's the most reasonable change in the flagship's foot traffic versus last year?
options: About 0.9x
About 1.2x
About 12x
About 2.2x
explain: The book says foot traffic reached 2.2x last year's, matching the big sales jump. Scaling one store into a district-wide movement brought real crowds through the door.
source: Resonating with Society's Pulse: Building Socially Conscious Brand Impact

context: Merkle's 2024 white paper on member data asset management says companies face serious challenges in how they organize member data and CX (customer experience) management: data resources and CX work are scattered across departments, making a unified strategy hard. The survey also found only 42% of companies make the CRM or CX team the core of cross-team work.
q: Based on these clues, what's the most reasonable estimate for the share of companies saying their current structure can't fully support data-driven CX?
options: About 57%
About 17%
About 27%
About 92%
explain: The book says about 57% say their current structure can't fully support it, which lines up with only 42% making CRM or CX the core of cross-team work. The bottleneck is mostly organizational design.
source: Member Data Asset Management and Trends in CX-Led Organizational Design

context: The book describes Dentsu's B2B2S philosophy: help clients grow their business, and in turn help that business make a positive impact on society. Following this, Dentsu Taiwan launched a media carbon accounting and carbon inventory program, verified by TUV Rheinland, making it the first marketing communications group to earn a certain international standard.
q: Given what a carbon inventory involves, which certification is it most likely to be?
options: ISO 9001 quality management
ISO 14001 environmental management
ISO 14064-1 GHG inventory
ISO 50001 energy management
explain: The book says Dentsu Taiwan became the first marketing communications group certified to ISO 14064-1 for greenhouse gas inventories. A carbon inventory measures greenhouse gas emissions, so it maps to the inventory standard, not a general environmental or energy management system.
source: Unlocking the Secrets of Media Carbon Accounting

context: The book sums up Dentsu Intelligence Center's "5M" ideas for generative AI. One of them, Make Your Own Model, argues that anyone can use general-purpose models, so a competitive edge comes from training on data others can't get. For example, when one customer says "search is so inconvenient" and another says "today is inconvenient for delivery," the model must tell apart the emotion and intent. Dentsu's role here is to bring in a data advantage clients don't have themselves.
q: According to the book, what core data does Dentsu use to build a custom AI model for a client?
options: Client's own POS sales and CRM member data
Platform-provided GA4 and LINE dashboard data
Industry research data published by IAB and BCG
Dentsu's proprietary CCS values and DAC browsing data
explain: The book says the idea uses Dentsu's proprietary CCS (consumer lifestyle and values data) plus DAC (web browsing behavior data) to build custom AI models that give clients a competitive edge.
source: Seeing 100 Times the Hope

context: Per the Ministry of Education's Sports Administration, after the pandemic eased in 2022, total public sports spending returned to pre-pandemic levels at NT$100.52B, up 15.6%. The book splits sports spending into four categories: sports events and media, sports gear, participatory sports, and esports. Activities that require showing up and taking part in person were hit hardest during the pandemic, and while sports events and media grew 17.1%, it still wasn't the fastest-growing category.
q: You need to pick the spending category that best rides this rebound for a sports brand. Based on these clues, which category grew the most?
options: Esports
Participatory sports
Sports gear
Sports events and media
explain: The book says participatory sports grew the most, up 30.7%, showing that after the pandemic people didn't just return to the stands but wanted to get out and play themselves.
source: Sports Marketing or Marketing Sports?

context: Starting in 2020, Google pushed Privacy Sandbox and prepared to phase out third-party cookies in Chrome. After four years of work, it made a major announcement on July 22, 2024 that the digital ad industry saw as great news. Still, the book argues brands must fully enter a low-cookie era, because more and more consumers use browsers that block cookies.
q: Based on these clues, what did Google announce, and what's the most reasonable response for brands?
options: It dropped the phaseout, but brands should still prep for a low-cookie era
Full phaseout in 2025, so brands should stop retargeting ads right away
It dropped the phaseout, so brands can go back to relying on third-party cookies
Phaseout in the EU only, so brands just need to adjust European campaigns
explain: The book says Google announced Chrome would drop its plan to phase out third-party cookies and keep supporting them, but industry experts note that as more consumers use blocking tools, tracking signals will keep weakening.
source: Digital Twins: The Hybrid Edge of Brand Power and Data Power

context: Honda dealers close up to 70% of in-store visits, but the problem was that showroom visits dropped sharply after the pandemic. Dentsu Kuohua found that 51% of people buy a car because friends or family recommend it, so it created "Veteran Drivers Recommend": owners used AI face swap to put friends and family into CR-V scenes and sent them invitations, backed by a referral reward. In eight weeks, over 130K people took part and 668 prospects came in for test drives.
q: Based on the high in-store close rate and the number of test drives, what's the most reasonable estimate of the sales growth the campaign drove?
options: About 0.3%
About 3%
About 270%
About 27%
explain: The book says the campaign drove 27% sales growth, and the brand later made this O2O campaign a regular sales model. The key was getting people into the showroom first, then handing them to high-closing sales staff.
source: Next-Level Imaging Power That Multiplies Creative Possibilities

context: A retail media network (RMN) is a retailer's business of selling ad space to brands. It covers on-site ads on the retailer's own channels and off-site ads bought from outside platforms. BCG compared gross margins across retail categories: traditional categories like beauty, home goods, department stores, and groceries sit around 19% to 38%, and off-site ads around 20% to 40%. On-site ads need no stock purchasing, inventory, or logistics, and the ad space runs on the retailer's own traffic.
q: Based on these clues, what range is the gross margin on RMN on-site ads most likely to fall in?
options: Under 10%
explain: The book cites a BCG chart showing on-site ad margins of 70% to 90%, far above off-site ads and other retail categories, which is one reason retailers are keen to invest in retail media.
source: Reaching the Summit of the Retail Media Kingdom

context: The book contrasts two views of competition. A "finite game" is like a sports match, with clear rules and an end. An "infinite game" is how business really works: there's no finish line, and players come and go at any time. Facing a falling birth rate, LEGO didn't just fight other toys for kids. It stuck to "limited bricks, infinite possibilities" and expanded into collectibles and home decor, opening an adult market that became a key growth source, while kids remain its core base.
q: Given this shift, what's the most reasonable estimate of adult LEGO's share of total sales today?
options: One-fiftieth
One-fifth
One-half
Four-fifths
explain: The book says adult LEGO now accounts for one-fifth of total sales. Infinite game thinking let LEGO break out of the kids-only frame, so the toy market didn't stall as birth rates fell.
source: Turning the Tide with Grit Amid Endless Change

context: HeySong's "Voice Beasts" put generative AI into vending machines: say what's on your mind into your phone, and you summon your own AI beast that "eats" your message and keeps evolving. The insight came from research showing Gen Z has the highest loneliness score of any group, has no one to talk to, and would rather open up to virtual characters than to real people.
q: Choosing where to debut this interactive game, which plan best matches what the book describes?
options: Only a few university campuses, aimed squarely at students
All convenience stores nationwide at once for max reach
Pop-ups in department stores to draw in families
A pilot in office buildings focused on stress relief for workers
explain: The book says it debuted at NTU, FCU, and NKUST only, giving students a way to voice their feelings and ease campus stress, and drew nearly 30,000 messages and 50,000+ shares.
source: Combining AI and Gen Z Insight to Strengthen Brands' Emotional Connection

context: The book holds up Nutter Butter as a model of “convergence”: a 50-plus-year-old American peanut butter cookie that most people had forgotten. With no ad budget, it posted absurd, illogical short videos on TikTok, layered with hidden codes and connected storylines, and built the Nutterverse, which young people shared, imitated, and co-created on their own. Another award-winning case in the same chapter, covered by media in 102 countries, earned about 330M impressions.
q: Based on these clues, what order of magnitude best fits what this zero-budget effort achieved?
options: About 250M impressions, tens of millions of engagements
About 25M impressions, millions of engagements
About 2.5M impressions, hundreds of thousands of engagements
About 2.5B impressions, hundreds of millions of engagements
explain: The book says Nutter Butter earned 249M impressions and 15M engagements with zero budget, on par with a global award winner, by being weird, genuine, and fun rather than loud.
source: “From Division to Convergence, the Evolution of Creativity”: Nutter Butter, “Are You OK?”

context: Dentsu Japan's “SATO 2531”: Japanese law requires married couples to share a surname, but doesn't say it must be the husband's. Working with researchers, the team projected that if nothing changes, everyone in Japan will be named Sato (the country's most common surname) by 2531. For that projection to hold, the name change has to fall almost entirely on women.
q: Based on these clues, what's the most reasonable estimate of the share of Japanese women who take their husband's surname?
