options: About 50%, roughly split between spouses
About 95%, the vast majority take his name
About 75%, most but with many exceptions
100%, the law says it must be his name
explain: The book says 95% of Japanese women take their husband's surname; “SATO 2531” projected a single national surname from this, drawing coverage in 102 countries and a UN recommendation that Japan amend the law within two years.
source: “From Division to Convergence, the Evolution of Creativity”: Dentsu Japan, “SATO 2531”

context: The book unpacks the myth that “TV is too expensive”: TV reaches huge audiences at once, so the broader you buy, the lower the cost per thousand impressions (CPM); its economics come from scale. Digital CPM is set by auction, and tighter targeting pushes the price up. YouTube ad CPMs typically run 80–250.
q: Your brand wants to reach a broad audience aged 30 and older. Per the book's estimate, where is TV CPM most likely to land?
options: About 250, just above YouTube's upper end
About 150, mid-range for YouTube
About 48, far below YouTube's range
About 500, over twice YouTube's level
explain: The book estimates TV CPM at only about 48 when targeting 30+; only when narrowed to a slice like ages 30–39 does it rise to about 247, slightly above YouTube.
source: “Cracking the Data Traps of Video Ads”: TV's Five Myths, Myth 2

context: More and more Taiwanese women freeze their eggs to keep the option of motherhood open. But the current Assisted Reproduction Act says a single woman must first marry and get her husband's consent before using her own eggs. So Dentsu Taiwan's “Unfreeze My Rights” staged a Mother's Day street campaign in which a middle-aged woman publicly sought a man just to provide the legally required signature.
q: Given this legal restriction, what's the most reasonable estimate of how many women who froze their eggs actually used them?
options: About half; most eventually use them
About 30%; some use them after marrying
About 20%; the law has limited impact
Under 10%; most are blocked by the law
explain: The book says only 8% used their own eggs, not by choice but because of the Act's marriage and spousal-consent requirement; the campaign pushed the Ministry of Health and Welfare to start drafting an amendment.
source: “From Division to Convergence, the Evolution of Creativity”: Dentsu Taiwan, “Unfreeze My Rights”

context: The book notes that in 2019 Adidas publicly reflected that over-relying on digital performance ads had produced great short-term conversion numbers but eroded brand reach and long-term memorability. Its brand-to-performance budget split was then about 23%/77%, so it decided to overhaul its strategy.
q: Based on the book, which split did Adidas most likely move to?
options: 60% Branding / 40% Performance, big on mass media
23% Branding / 77% Performance, with tighter targeting
40% Branding / 60% Performance, a modest brand boost
100% Branding / 0% Performance, all performance paused
explain: The book says that from 2019 Adidas shifted the split from 23%/77% to 60%/40%, returning to core brand values and the power of mass media.
source: “Cracking the Data Traps of Video Ads”: The New Reality of Media Buying

context: Merkle argues that traditional GA (Google Analytics) records behavior such as clicks, time on site, and conversions. The book says brands must move from being “conversion-rate driven” to “building deep relationships,” which means asking why customers make a choice, where they drop off, and what needs fixing. To do this, it proposes an upgraded XGA.
q: Given this direction, what does the X in XGA most reasonably stand for?
options: Extra: adding more tracking tags
Experience: flow and interaction quality
Express: faster conversion reporting
Extend: tracking across more platforms
explain: The book says XGA is Experience GA: it looks at experience-flow design and the quality of value interactions, acting as a gauge and tuner for interaction quality rather than just collecting more data.
source: “The Customer Journey in the XGA Era”

context: When LEGO weighed building a factory in Asia in 2012, it used scenario planning, sorting each issue by likelihood (high or low) and speed of change (fast or slow) into four priorities: ACT (act now), ADAPT (adjust gradually), PREPARE (plan for contingencies), and PARK (hold off). The book also suggests using AI to simulate a backup plan for each change, so you aren't guessing when the market actually shifts.
q: You judge that “a major ad platform's costs suddenly spike” is unlikely, but if it happens it will hit your budget fast. Under this framework, what's the most reasonable classification and response?
options: ACT: move budget off that platform now
ADAPT: shift the media mix each quarter
PREPARE: simulate a backup platform plan
PARK: note it and just keep monitoring
explain: The book defines PREPARE as issues that are unlikely but fast-moving and need a contingency plan, and suggests preparing for changes like a sudden Meta cost spike by estimating Google and TV performance in advance.
source: Editor's Letter: “Opportunity Favors the Prepared ‘Super Brain’”

context: 91APP says generative AI has built a “GAI wall”: consumers now do their discovery through feeds, chatbots, and AI agents, and rarely start browsing from a brand's homepage. But for transactions such as purchases and bookings, they still have to leave the walled garden for the brand's D2C site, leaving behind the brand's own first-party data.
q: Given this view, which kind of page should a brand invest in most on its D2C site?
options: Homepage: brand image and entry navigation
Navigation page: browse the site level by level
Blog: more content to win search rankings
Product page: capture sales traffic from AI
explain: The book says “ads are traffic” has given way to “products are traffic”: what matters most on a D2C site is no longer the homepage or navigation but the product page, the battleground and source of first-party data.
source: “From the Open Web to Walled Gardens: A New Internet Reshaped by AI”

context: In “Creativity ++,” Dentsu says brands now face not just marketing optimization but a full rebuild of their business models. A “siloed agency model” splits creative, media, and data among different agencies, each working on its own. Citing the 2024 CMO REPORT, the book notes that in the same survey 82% of companies expect agencies to integrate all capabilities seamlessly.
q: Based on these clues, what's the most reasonable estimate of the share of companies that say the siloed agency model no longer meets their needs?
options: About 78%
About 28%
About 48%
About 98%
explain: The book says 78% of companies find the siloed agency model no longer enough, close to the 82% who want integration, which is why Dentsu proposes Creativity ++ transformational creativity.
source: “Creativity ++: Transformational Creativity Builds Ecosystems for Brands”

context: Citing Ministry of Finance data, the book says Taiwan's beauty industry grew only 0.1% in 2023–24. Makeup and skincare is still the largest category, but its share is shrinking and its growth slowing. The author sees this not as simple saturation but as category shift: consumers now pursue an “all-around feeling of beauty” that goes beyond visible makeup to something more inward. The book names two new growth engines: fragrance (up 9.2%) and an even faster-growing everyday category that extends from the face to the whole body.
q: You need to pick the category with the highest 2024 growth for a beauty group to invest more in. Based on the book's data, which should you choose?
options: Makeup and skincare
Face and body cleansers
Hair care
Fragrance
explain: The book says cleansers grew 15.6% in 2024, outpacing fragrance's 9.2%, reflecting consumers broadening their beauty spending toward more inward, varied experiences.
source: “The Beauty Experience Era: Beauty Brands' Strategy Within the Beauty Ecosystem”

context: dentsu SPECTRUM is Dentsu's programmatic premium ad offering in Taiwan. It uses PMP (private marketplace) deals to ensure placement quality and brand safety, and has expanded step by step like a “spectrum”: Premium Display in 2015, then Video in 2017. When the pandemic hit in 2020 and consumers vanished from the streets to stay home all day, SPECTRUM quickly extended its reach from personal devices to audiences counted by household.
q: Given this situation, which ad type did SPECTRUM most likely add in 2020?
options: Podcast: audio ads heard on the commute
DOOH: digital screens on streets and transit
CTV: ads on connected TVs in the living room
LINE Official Account: one-to-one push messages
explain: The book says that during the 2020 pandemic SPECTRUM connected CTV (connected TV), extending reach into living rooms, so its five types became Premium, Video, CTV, DOOH, and Performance.
source: “The Quality and Trends of the Digital Ad Ecosystem, Through SPECTRUM”

context: A Brand Lift study splits viewers into an “exposed group” that saw the ad and a “control group” that didn't, then compares their awareness and favorability; it claims the split is random. The book warns that digital video is usually sold on CPV (cost per view), so ad systems prioritize users “likely to watch in full,” and the result is only an in-platform comparison.
q: A Brand Lift report for a YouTube campaign shows a big jump in favorability. What's the most reasonable reading?
options: Random splits remove bias, so it's proof of impact
It proves YouTube beats TV, so shift budget
The control group saw more ads, so it's understated
It may just light up existing fans; cross-check it
explain: The book says people who already like the brand and often watch ads in full are more likely to land in the exposed group, so lift may just “light up people who already support you,” and it can't be compared across platforms.
source: “Cracking the Data Traps of Video Ads,” Observation 2: Good Brand Lift Numbers Don't Mean Real Results

context: Dentsu's People Model fine-tunes AI on its large annual consumer survey to build AI Personas (digital twins of consumers), each mapped to a real respondent. Backtested against real answers held out of training, the simulation correlates with real results at 0.89 (out of 1.0): items people rate high, the twins rate high too.
q: After seeing this, a client's CMO says: “So the simulation is only off by 11% on average. We can skip real-person surveys before launches from now on.” Based on the book, how would you respond?
options: Agree. 0.89 is close to perfect, so it can replace pre-launch real-person surveys
Disagree. 0.89 isn't high enough, so the simulation shouldn't inform decisions yet
Correlation shows matching trends, not an error rate. Simulate to screen, but keep real people for big calls
First push the correlation above 0.95, then start using the simulation for any decision
explain: The book states a correlation coefficient isn't an error rate, so “1 - 0.89” doesn't mean an 11% gap. It recommends simulating to screen and using real people to verify, never letting simulation alone decide a launch.
source: The Agentic Era: The Real Distance Between Brands and People / [Special Feature] People Model

context: People Model is built on Dentsu's CCS consumer survey: people in Taiwan aged 15 to 74, quota-sampled by gender, age and region, with 5,045 valid responses. This design represents the overall market well, but the narrower the segment, the fewer responses it gets.
q: A private bank wants to use People Model to simulate how “high-net-worth individuals” would react to a new wealth service. Based on the book's advice, what's the most sensible approach?
options: First check whether sample coverage is enough, and add small real-person research if needed
Just simulate it. 5,045 responses are enough to represent any segment
Have a general-purpose AI role-play wealthy clients to fill the gap the survey leaves
Drop the simulation and go back to a months-long traditional large-scale survey
explain: The book admits CCS represents the population well, but for niche targets like specific professions or high-net-worth groups, the system flags sample coverage and suggests adding small real-person research rather than forcing a fit.
source: [Special Feature] People Model

context: The 37th Golden Melody Awards in 2026 averaged a 3.37 TV rating, a clear rebound from 2.31 the year before and above the 2.78 of the year before that. YouTube livestream views also hit a recent high. The book notes that as media fragments, a work can be a hit in its own circle while people outside it never encounter it.
q: According to the book's analysis, what was most likely the key reason ratings recovered?
options: Classic singers returned in force, replacing new-generation work with nostalgia
Familiar classics shared the stage with new acts, so every age group found a way in
Stronger livestreams and social clips pulled young viewers back to TV
A tighter, shorter ceremony made viewers less likely to change the channel
explain: The book stresses it wasn't just “classic singers came back.” The show didn't replace the present with the past; a Familiar × New design let different generations share the same stage.
source: From the Golden Melody Awards to Empresses in the Palace: The Brand Value of Shared Memories

context: Dentsu's “2025 CMO Report” surveyed over 1,950 CMOs across 14 countries and regions; 89% agree agentic AI will have a major impact on business. As AI agents start gathering information, comparing prices and filtering options for consumers, the report also notes that in an agentic AI world, some human-side brand qualities become even more important.
q: The CEO plans to shift most of the brand budget to AI search optimization, saying “getting recommended by AI is enough.” Based on the report's conclusions, which judgment makes the most sense?
options: Agree. AI agents compare specs and prices rationally, so brand image won't matter
Agree, and also switch all ads to AI-generated content to cut production costs
Pause AI investment and decide the budget once agentic AI goes mainstream
Optimize for AI, but keep investing in trust, taste and brand preference
explain: The report says trust and taste matter more than ever in the agentic AI era, and 90% of CMOs believe strong brand preference is key to winning. The book adds that brands must give people a reason to choose them before AI steps in to compare prices.
source: Agents of Growth: Growth Drivers in the Age of AI Agents

context: Dentsu Creative's “Growth Triangle” maps three challenges brands face on the AI-shaped consumer journey: win the algorithm means being correctly understood and recommended by AI; win hearts means building trust and preference in human decisions; win culture means entering the culture and building long-term, deep brand equity.
q: A beverage brand often shows up in AI assistant recommendations and has steady member repurchases, but almost nobody talks about it, remixes it or treats it as a topic. Under the Growth Triangle, which side should it strengthen next?
options: Win the algorithm: keep optimizing content structure and data signals
Win hearts: invest more in membership and one-to-one relationships
Win culture: become something people talk about and take part in
All three are covered: move budget back to performance ads for short-term sales
explain: The book notes that brands stuck at feature comparisons are easily swapped out by algorithms. They need to enter the culture and become something people discuss, join in and identify with, a preference no single campaign can create.
source: Agents of Growth: Growth Drivers in the Age of AI Agents

context: Carat says People Intelligence (PI) has three core capabilities: Sense (perception and insight) spots the problem; Connect (creation and linkage) ties strategy, creative, media and data together to solve it; Judge (judgment and decisions) tells true from false and sets priorities. The book also notes that generative AI is good at generating, not verifying.
q: After adopting AI agents, a team gathers data and drafts proposals several times faster. The manager is deciding where to focus people. Based on the book, which setup makes the most sense?
options: Let AI share Sense and Connect while people focus on verifying and final calls
People focus on Sense to gather insights, then hand the final call to AI to optimize
People focus on Connect's creative integration, and automated data systems make the calls
Hand all three to AI, with people only checking formats and managing delivery dates
explain: The book argues “leave execution to AI”: the core of PI is to judge. AI can help with Sense and Connect, but judgment is the capability a company should least give away.
source: “Judgment” Will Be the Scarcest Edge

context: Generative AI makes assets faster and in greater volume, but it also brings a flood of look-alike “AI Slop”: the more content, the harder the brand is to recognize. Dentsu Taiwan's SLIP framework puts AI into a disciplined production line in four steps: Spec (standardizing), Line (production lines), Inspection (checks) and Pattern (repeatable models).
q: The team's brief to AI is a single line: “Make a youthful social post for us.” Everything it produces is bland and doesn't feel like the brand. From the SLIP perspective, where does the problem most likely start, and what should be fixed first?
options: The model isn't capable enough. Switch to a stronger generative AI tool
The spec is unclear. Write a production spec defining tone and red lines
The prompt isn't clever enough. Have someone refine it and rerun
Too few outputs. Generate many variants and pick the best one
explain: The book says AI Slop usually starts not with weak models but with unclear specs. Many companies think the core asset of the AI era is the prompt, but the Spec (production spec) matters more.
source: Defining “Asset Output Standards”: Turning AI's Generative Power into a Brand's Delivery Power

context: Citing a Nikkei xTREND model, the book says the consumer journey is shifting from AISAS (Attention, Interest, Search, Action, Share) to AICAS. AICAS no longer starts with passively receiving ads; it starts with consumers actively asking AI “Which brand is right for me?” For smaller brands, buying enough media exposure to “break the surface” often takes more budget than they can handle.
q: A skincare brand on a limited budget wants to get picked during this shift. What's the most sensible next step?
options: Pour the budget into more impressions so consumers notice the brand first
Go all in on search keyword ads to grab the top search result
Cut content production and move everything into promotions and discounts
Build clear, credible, AI-citable content and social word of mouth
explain: The book notes that brands without clear, credible, citable content may be dropped from the answer before comparison even begins. Social word of mouth and AI summaries can push a brand onto the shortlist through user sharing and AI citations.
source: Stop Buying Impressions, Start Buying Attention

context: Taiwan officially became a super-aged society in 2025: one in every five people is 65 or older. Life insurers have long relied on anxiety and fear to drive decisions. The book argues that in an era when AI can mass-produce content, what people really buy is “emotional self-identity,” and brands ultimately compete on who can create emotional preference.
q: You're planning communication on aging for a life insurance brand. Based on Nan Shan Life's “Centenarian Life” case in the book, which direction fits best?
options: Neither stoke fear nor glamorize aging; show everyday reality and grow it into a public conversation
Stress the risk numbers for medical and long-term care costs to push people to buy coverage soon
Film inspiring stories of seniors chasing dreams to build a positive image of old age
Use AI to generate many versions of aging-themed ads and target them by segment
explain: Nan Shan Life “told no inspirational stories and didn't glamorize old age,” taking viewers into daily life to see that older people are all around them. The project then grew into “Learning to Age” forums, health events and financial education, turning one ad into a societal conversation.
source: The Power of Authenticity, Being Redefined

context: The author, a former Apple Daily reporter, argues that once AI starts producing content, what disappears is the “cost of verification.” He recalls the newsroom's logic: one source may have an agenda, adding another may still be biased, and credibility only starts when the next independent source points to the same fact.
q: You want to quote a market figure from an AI summary in a pitch. By the author's verification standard, at least how many independent sources pointing to the same fact do you need for it to hold up?
options: One authoritative source
Two sources that agree
Three independent sources
Five or more sources
explain: The Apple Daily rule was that every news story needed at least three sources to cross-check; credibility only starts when a third independent source points to the same fact.
source: Why Trust Is the Hardest Edge to Copy in the AI Era

context: Dentsu Japan made a Reiwa-era MV of ORANGE RANGE's 2007 hit “Ikenai Taiyou,” deliberately targeting people of the team's own generation. The book separates two kinds of nostalgia: a “memory hit” just makes people reminisce, while Shared Memory turns viewers from watchers into participants.
q: You also want to use 2000s nostalgia in a brand video. Based on this case, which design is most likely to get viewers participating on their own?
options: Go for a polished, fashionable Y2K look so every frame feels premium
Use only mainstream symbols everyone knows, so every age group gets it
Concentrate the budget on launch-day exposure to hit a single-day peak
Pack in many specific, recognizable everyday details for viewers to decode
explain: The team avoided a pretty Y2K look and packed in 72 specific “Heisei references” like hibiscus flowers and carton milk tea. Viewers hunted for and cataloged them, even adding details that appeared by chance, turning nostalgia into Shared Memory.
source: From the Golden Melody Awards to Empresses in the Palace: The Brand Value of Shared Memories

context: Dentsu Intelligence Center splits an agent's permissions on the consumer journey into four layers: observe/understand (read data, identify needs), recommend (compare, rank and suggest), decide (pick the next step for the user under set rules) and act (write to systems, build carts, place orders). The book also warns that agents amplify a company's existing capabilities, and messy data gets amplified too.
q: A health supplement brand hasn't finished filling in product ingredient attributes, and its return rules are spread across three systems. Yet the owner wants the agent to place replenishment orders for customers from day one. What's the most sensible approach?
options: Open up to the act layer now and fix issues from customer complaints later
Start with observe and recommend, then step up once data and rollback are in place
Pause the whole agent project until every system is fully rebuilt
Open up to the decide layer and let the agent guess the missing ingredient data
explain: The book advises opening permissions step by step by risk, since more autonomy isn't always better. With attributes missing, an agent may put items without the needed ingredient into the cart, and companies needn't treat adoption as an all-or-nothing choice.
source: AI Agents Enter the Consumer Journey: How Health, Beauty, and Retail Turn AI into Action
